utterances.text: And did you personally attend the taking out of the licna karta or ID cards? You said that they were taken out of trousers that were found on the body. Did you attend this personally?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: The situation with the monitoring is, although you're non-interventionist and you're trying to get information, is also not to be obstructionist. I was -- always maintained a distance from it on the understanding that the information would be brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And please try and be very specific. Where was the licna karta, the ID card, found?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I can't be very specific. This function was carried out by members of the forensic team. I do not know which one. It is -- it was their site. It was their exhumation. It was up to them to retrieve it. It was my position to monitor this and to retrieve whatever information was obtained. I was not in their face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which other parts of the contents did you have in the place the ID card was found, the wallet?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood that it was found in a wallet. What else was there in the wallet? What other contents were in the wallet that you found the ID card in?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't find the ID card. The ID card was found by the forensic team. The details are on the index that are contained in the binder. I can't recollect what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're talking about that body, BA09. Did you carry out the identification of the body? Was the identification of the body carried out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these bodies have not been identified. An identification document was recovered and has been associated with body BA09.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they weren't identified. And what about the BA19 body? You say that from the clothing on the body, an ID card was retrieved, and it was in the name of Nexhadin Berisha with all the other specifications, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: That's the information that was passed to me at the time, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what part of the clothing was this ID card retrieved from?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't retrieve any of these documents. I didn't examine any of these documents. It was brought to my attention. These documents had been recovered. This was work carried out by the forensic team. It was up to them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the process of taking out the ID card from the clothing on the body that you're talking about, was that recorded using video technology?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I generally do not know, Your Honour. I'm assuming so. There was a crime technician there who took photographs. He also had a video camera. The directions given to him was given by the lead pathologist, in that case Professor Dunjic. He gave directions to the crime technician. I had no input in that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in what state was BA19 found?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but the photographs should be there. What I can say is all bodies were in quite advanced stage of decomposition. They were skeletal. There was some flesh. This is a general overview that I observed, but there was evidence of burning. This was just a very, very sorry mass of humanity that was dumped into one pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I then conclude that you were present at the moment when the ID card that you're talking about was taken out of the clothing found on this particular body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's really given his evidence as best he can about it. He was an overall observer and monitor of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you talk about identification documents later on which were found, as you say, in the dispersed clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: "Dispersed clothing." I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Scattered clothing.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I believe I referred to it as loose clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you then explain how this clothing was loose?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: The clothing was described by the forensic team as being loose clothing because it was not associated with a particular body or body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in what parts of the clothing were these documents found? Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't answer that question. Mr. Milosevic, I don't see the point of this cross-examination. The evidence is this: There is a mass grave. There are a number of bodies. In the clothing of the bodies there are found documents which relate to massacres or other missing persons in Kosovo. Now that is the evidence. It will be a matter for us at the end of the case to determine on that whether it supports the Prosecution argument that these bodies were brought from Kosovo and put into mass graves at these sites. Now, so far you've cross-examined for over half an hour, and we really have added nothing to the case at all. If you want to make submissions about the documents in the -- to us about the documents in the binder, you can do so, but on my calculation, you've got another quarter of an hour or 20 minutes at the most to cross-examine, and that would be more than sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean I have 15 to 20 minutes in all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is purely technical evidence. It seems to me we're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I just want to support what the Presiding Judge has said. I'm surprised that you're spending so much time on this cross-examination on what is a wholly technical matter. You should reserve your cross-examination for weightier subjects, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you claim that all the names mentioned from the documents you're talking about belong to people from the massacre in Suva Reka. And Mr. May just mentioned the word. And this dates to the 26th of March, 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I believe I said that all but one related to people from Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on what grounds is it claimed that there was a massacre in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was I who said it, not the witness. Now, go on with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The exhumations at the BA2 location, were you present there from the very beginning or did you join them at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I was there from the very beginning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, number 1, bodies from this locality, you talk about personal findings with Ismajl Laxhi [phoen], the 30th of June, born the 30th of June, 1938 in Tirana. And this was not attached to the body; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was this personal identification or personal sign, mark?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: It was identified to me as being a dog tag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it attached round the neck?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: It was not attached to a body, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean it wasn't attached to the body?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: It was loose, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, number 2, BA92, body number 2, you say you found the ID card in the name of Ali Bajrami. Where was that licna karta found? Was it attached to the body or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I didn't find licna karta. It's been reported to me that a licna karta was found in clothing of body 2 BA92.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what clothing was there on body number 3 in your statement, which is location 2 BA? And in your statement it is 2 BA117, in fact. That's the number you refer to the body by.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: That reference number was given by the forensic team and for how they were numbering it. I generally have no clue what clothing was on the body. If they told me that it was removed from clothing from the body that was given the number of 2 BA117, that is information that I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now we come to body number 4 in your statement, which is 2 BA117 [sic], you talk about a licna karta found in the name of Simon Sokoli. Where exactly was this ID card found and employment certificate from the Jateks Holding Corporation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to this body under number 5, you talk about things found relating to this body and then a second ID card, licna karta, with the surname Sokoli and the date of birth being the 31st of January, 1965; is that right? A second one was found?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what grounds do you claim that the clothing and things in which this licna karta was found belonged to the previous individual? How are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I don't claim any of this information, Your Honour. This is the information that was passed to me by members of the forensic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in what state were the bodily remains of body 6 in the portion of your statement that refers to site 2 BA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has already said that he cannot give evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was it a skeleton or a body? You say that a rucksack was found, that there was a rucksack there. Now, was it on a skeleton or were there tissues on the body?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: From my own recollection of seeing the bodies at the site, I can say generally that some were skeletal, some had -- were reasonably well preserved. Some did have flesh on them. Whether that refers to the body that the accused is talking about, I genuinely cannot say, Your Honour. These bodies, again, as an overview, had been -- there was a number of tyres sticking out of the grave itself. There was evidence of burning. There was commingling. There was a lot of fractures and loose limbs. I cannot be any more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what else was found in the rucksack that you recovered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't recover it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then, the rucksack that was found.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about number 7? The site was 2 BA221. You state that an ID card was found in the name of Gjon Hasanaj, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: I think that refers to his father's name, Seyt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when this document was found, this identification document? Were you present at the time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Yes, I would have been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that the ID card was found on the body. That's right, isn't it? What part of the body was it found on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't claim any of this. This is the information that was given to me by the members of the forensic team who were carrying out the exhumations, carrying out the post-mortems, and carrying out the evidential recording of whatever was found. This is their information that was passed to me. I don't know how to make this any clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need. You've made it perfectly clearly, Mr. Fulton, but we'll continue with this cross-examination until it finishes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The forester -- the summary that was distributed to us prior to your testimony, on page 1 of that, it says under the subheading "Mass Graves in Serbia," and it was handed in in English only, it says the following: "It was believed that [in English] bodies transported from Kosovo to Belgrade --" [interpretation] and this next bit is vital -- [in English] "of campaign seeking to erase -- to erase the traces of the crimes committed in Kosovo." [Interpretation] On what grounds do you state that this was a campaign to erase the traces of the crimes committed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: This appears to have been a view that is held by the investigating police officer and can be found in many of his press releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it established who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't answer that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're a professional policeman. You've been a professional policeman for 20 years now, as you said yourself, and now I'm asking you, in view of your professional experience: Do you believe that somebody could conceive of such nonsense, that during the war when many people are losing their lives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a proper question. First of all, the witness's beliefs are not relevant. Secondly, this is a matter of argument which you can address to us, Mr. Milosevic, but there's no point asking the witness about it. He is not here -- let me continue because it is a general point. Witnesses are not here to argue a case. That is the Prosecutor's job, and you will have the opportunity to rebut it in due course. Witnesses are merely here to give evidence of what they saw or heard or know about, and your cross-examination should be so directed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is so directed, Mr. May, because in this paper that was provided before this witness was brought in, it says that there was some kind of a campaign. If you mean that -- if you're trying to say that the Serbs are that stupid to believe that somebody, during the war, would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to listen to these arguments now. What the witness says when giving evidence from the witness chair there is what's evidence. It's not what is in these summaries. These summaries are not evidence. This isn't part of the evidence. In any event, I allowed you to ask a question since it was there, but the witness has dealt with it as best he can. Now, have you got anything else that you want to ask the witness about his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say that it is in the summary, well it says in the summary that it is part of a campaign. Can it also say in the summary that this is perhaps rigged up? Perhaps it's a frame-up, a malicious frame-up, not this kind of rubbish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to go on with this. You can argue the case in due course. Do the amici have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You have wasted the time of the Court already. Now, Ms. Romano, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness mentioned the name of the investigative police officer who held that opinion. I would just like to ask the witness if he knows the name of this police officer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ROBERT FULTON
utterances.text: It's Captain Dragan Karleusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just would like to know if the statement has been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it hasn't. It should get a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fulton, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is the investigator Barney Kelly, and Mr. Nice will take the witness. They're coming. We just need one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Actually, can the witness stay outside for a minute? I didn't realise he was being summoned. Your Honour, we come now to witnesses who deal specifically with the village of Racak. I know that the Court has got the witness statement of the next witness, Barney Kelly. I hope it's also had and been able to lay its hands on his full report which was served earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the one attached to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so, yes. It's about that thick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's called an assessment, just to make sure we have the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's called an assessment, absolutely right. And indeed, very conveniently, on the fourth sheet in, it sets out where Racak features in the indictment, paragraphs 98 and thereabouts. An issue I think may arise as to the proper scope of this witness's evidence, and I'm approaching it on the basis that an issue will arise, and of course it's perhaps interesting to observe that whereas I'm often saying in procedural matters that the reason for procedural departure or departure from some procedural norms is because the field of evidence in relation to the case generally is infinite as opposed to finite, in Racak, we actually have an incident where there is probably a finite, although substantial, field of evidence, but it is a field of evidence realistically far too large to be handled in full by this Tribunal in the time available for its consideration. That observation may be made about many, if not all, of the locations to which the Chamber will have to give consideration in this part of the trial and, of course, in the Croatian and Bosnian parts as well. So the issue that we face is one of general importance. Racak itself is of significance not just because it features in the indictment in the way it does, but because it was, of course, a turning point around which NATO made its decision to bomb Kosovo. And it's plainly significant to the Defence, in light of the cross-examination and the issues that appear to be being raised about whether the bodies were killed in the way their position would suggest or in some other way. And thus it is that the possibility of the Chamber having access to a summary of the evidence overall is important for this part of this case. It's important for issues of timetable for this part of the case. In our respectful submission, it's important for the integrity of a judgement to be delivered in due course that should be able to point to consideration of more rather than less material; and it's important for the Tribunal generally, maybe, and for other cases where similar issues arise. As I said earlier, this Tribunal, slightly differently constituted, has explored this matter before, and I'm not going to repeat the jurisprudence to which you referred there, but at the end of the evidence that I want to call before concluding my submissions, I'll take you to just a few other bits of jurisprudence that I've been helpfully provided with and can turn you to which may assist. But of course, it's under our Rules that the decision has to be made whether summarising evidence can be available. What I would now ask is that the witness comes in and gives the evidence of geography, which he would probably have to give in any event, identifying the various crime locations - and let me be quite clear that the purpose of this evidence will be or include revelation to the Chamber of the complexity of the Racak incident, which for the reasons I have explained you're going to have to consider - and the difficulties, or it may be impossibilities, of dealing with that evidence on the limited number of witnesses that it's going to be possible for us to call. I'm also going to draw an analogy between his evidence and the material that is available to the Court already in the OSCE report As Seen As Told. We'll have a short look at that with the witness. The witness has some very large plans of which we already have small copies. I think arrangements have been made for a blackboard to be produced but we haven't got one yet. Oh, dear. If Ms. Graham could give me the number of the same maps. 94 tab 73 is the small one, I believe. If the witness can come in with his maps, we'll see if we can position them somewhere, perhaps on a chair, for him to point to if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are some photographs which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are lots of photographs in the album. I'll ask him to refer to some of those although, again, to save time, it may be less rather than more in number. And to some degree I will be guided by the degree of detail that the Court perhaps is able to indicate it finds helpful. But it is a complex story or complicated story and familiarity with the geography will probably be, as so often with reconnaissance, time well spent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I would like you to clarify something for me, please. Again we have officials from the Office of the Prosecutor appearing here, and they're supposed to be some kind of witnesses. This witness is supposed to testify now. He's an investigator, and in his statement, he gives assessments that are exclusively within the scope of the court. Secondly, he testifies to the interviews he had with the witnesses and that their statements are consistent in many aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I'm going to interrupt you to explain what is going to happen. The witness is going to give evidence about geography and about the photographs which he took. He can do that. He's entitled to do that. He was there and he knows about it. As for the other matters, there will then be legal argument as to whether he can give evidence about them or not. And before we make a decision on that, we will hear you. So let the witness be sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could very kindly bring in the two large maps that are on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The usher is very kindly bringing in the large maps. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Has the smaller version of them been found? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Barney Kelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Occupation and, in a sentence, your background experience?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I'm an investigator. I am a member of the Irish police force. I've been in the investigative role for the last 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You joined the OTP when?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I joined the OTP on the 15th of September, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you charged with investigating and preparing a report or reports on Racak?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is it your that the Chamber has, described as an assessment?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of your work, have you been able to mark on the large overhead map which is to your right, and I think we're waiting for an easel at the moment.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll look at it in two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry about this delay, Your Honour. No doubt my mistake. I thought I'd made arrangements for an easel to come but it hasn't arrived yet. Can we therefore lay on the ELMO until we have an easel which will be capable of being captured by the cameras --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To save time, Mr. Kelly, would you just turn round and get the larger of those two maps for us. Turn it around so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that's visible to the Court from there. It looks as though Judge Robinson may not be able to see it from there. Let's see if it turns up on the video. I wonder if the cameras could focus on that and see if they can pick it up for us, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does this show Racak and its surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're going to have your keep your mouth close enough to the microphone. There's a pointer there which is extending. Thank you very much. I hope this works. The village is the village of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No. The village is the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right, the municipality is the municipality of Stimlje. Just point that out to us.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: In order to do that I would have to show you the other map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. We've got the wrong one first. Can you put the other one on, please. All right. Thank you. Right. The municipality is Stimlje. Just point that out.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is the entire town and municipality of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the cameras could help us with that. If you wouldn't mind just focusing and leaving it on there, thank you. There is, I think, three routes into Racak, one of which is the principal road. Please point that out for us.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That is this road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It goes down --

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It goes right down and then you must take a right-hand turn at this point and then continue into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. We've heard about a hospital or a mental hospital that features in some of the evidence. Just point out where that is, please.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. That's at number 4, this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other two routes into Racak which merge into a single lane, point those out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That is this road here, which if you follow it up through the sign of Racak, it comes from the -- again the main road to Prizren and the main road to Pristina which goes through the town of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Put that first map on, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Focus on that, please. Again you have to have the microphone sufficiently close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, Usher, could you move the plan nearer to the witness so that he can be heard while he's pointing to the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you sit down, please, Mr. Kelly. The audio-visual booth would be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could focus on that for us. Can the audio-visual give us that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've shown us the other road in, and that's marked -- they're not marked, but they're more minor roads, I think, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. The second of these minor roads is this road here, which again is further up heading towards Prizren, and it intersects then with the other road which is nearer the mental institute. And they cross at one point, but they both lead into the village of Racak and approximately at the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you understand at this stage of your evidence I'm not asking you for any account that other people gave you. Do you follow that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just want geographical locations, although, of course, to some degree they're built on other people's evidence, but nevertheless. What you've marked here, and we'll look at it very swiftly and then turn to the other map, you've marked number 1, which is the power station?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's probably helpful if the audio-visual stays on the map for this but it's a matter for them. But number 1, the power station. Thank you. Number 2, the municipal buildings. I'm not too troubled with those. Number 3, in the same general area, we have the MUP compound. Have you been to the MUP compound?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it the only MUP compound in the area or is there more than one such?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No. It is the only compound in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know if that deals with the -- with both branches of the MUP or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four, you've told us is the asylum. Just point that out again.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This large area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to move to the left of the map a little bit further to pick up 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. If the booth could help us with that.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This area here is number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Wait till we've got -- all right. Now, 5 is the house of Sadik Osmani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's just worth observing that the white line that's been drawn on what is an aerial photograph is something that has been drawn on, it's not a topographical feature, is it?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's right; I drew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may or may not tell us in due course what it is but that's something which has been drawn on. Six is the ravine in which the bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seven is something that has been identified as the KLA bunker, and that is something you've seen?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we have photographs of the bunker in the Racak binder, and we have photographs from the bunker, giving an idea of its view.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The proper term of address is "Your Honour," I think, here, if you don't mind. And we've heard some evidence of another line of fortifications. This bunker, did this show the signs of use; cigarette butts, things of that sort?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Not at the time I inspected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, did it have other appearances of use or not?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: There is -- there are -- there is testimony to the fact that, yes, it was in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Eight is the school, nine the mosque, and -- I'm not sure I need trouble with ten, so I won't. No, I'm not going to trouble with 10 nor the arrows. Going back, please, to 8 and 9, and then we'll turn to the other map. Can we go back to 8 and 9, please? If the audio-visual booth could take us back to 8 and 9, please. Thank you. As you come into the village from the south road, the main road, you pass the school and then you come to the mosque, and insofar as there's a centre to the village, does either of these indicate the centre or not or can you express a view?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: They wouldn't indicate the geographical centre but they would certainly indicate a pivotal centre, a religious centre, i.e., the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the audio-visual booth could help us just briefly by moving a little bit up on the map. The area in orange marked as "B" is one hill, and that's the hill of --?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's the hill of Cesta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further to the north, in a round orange marker, is the hill of?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Pisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And marked on the map to the east is the hill of?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Geshtenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That map, Your Honours, can be found in the Racak binder at tab 4. It's already been separately exhibited as Exhibit 94, tab 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can now look at the other map, which is of a smaller scale, a more detailed map. And before we do, could you please just tell us this about your investigation before we look at the map -- questions. In the course of your investigation, how many witness statements did you review?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Sixty-two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your statement, I think, refers to 60, 11 plus 49, but there were two others, were there?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's inclusive of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the initial stage of preparation of this case, how many were -- such statements were considered for presentation to court?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Approximately in the region of 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under further consideration by the lawyers then working in the team, to what number was this first further reduced?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It was then reduced to 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From 17 to?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Down to nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then, given the time constraints, from nine to what?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: To five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's five witnesses of the events in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are, in addition to that, other witnesses, one of whom from whom we've heard, General Drewienkiewicz, Ciaglinski, and people of that sort.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And other international observers. Your examination of the material identifies various sites that need to be considered, and you've described them on this map which is separately exhibited as 94, tab 73, I think. Sorry, is this one tab 73? They're both tab 73. You've identified six crime locations, but because some crime locations have more than one discrete scene, there are about 13 different scenes to be considered for an overall view of Racak?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may or may not be helpful to go through the photographs at this stage, but I'm not intending to do so in any degree slavishly, but I can at least identify where they are, or at least I hope I can. If the audio-visual booth would be good enough, please, to take us to the map now, focusing on the figure 1 and the surrounding area. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. If we can focus in on number 1. Thank you. It's worth observing now that the reference markings you've used have changed, because if we look not to 1 but just to the south and east of 1, we see a different symbol for something we've seen before, don't we, Mr. Kelly?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: We do indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've now, on this map, converted to using internationally recognised conventional signs?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The sign is?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This is the international symbol for mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although it's slightly off the screen at the moment, it doesn't matter, south of that we can see the international recognised sign for a school?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And to the left, the "P" sign is the internationally recognised sign for what?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: For headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what headquarters did you identify that as?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This -- identified this as the Racak KLA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right there in the centre part of town.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other element of geography simply now before I simply forget it. From a witness, General Drewienkiewicz, we heard evidence of and saw a videotape of fortifications in a different position from those that you described in the bunker, and we can see the bunker on the map, the bunker you described, at the bottom left-hand -- well, slightly to the left of the school sign, if the audio-visual booth would help.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: This area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the internationally recognised sign for what?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: For a bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see the little squiggly lines above it. Are those the bunker and other trenches that --

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, these lines, white on black, indicate the labyrinth of trenches that were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In addition to those, however, General Drewienkiewicz told us of fortifications that he found although he told us they hadn't necessarily been used. Did you see those yourself?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean at any stage, did you see them?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Not the ones he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where do you understand them to be, just to remind us?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: If you take a left from crime location 1 and you follow the little track that's there, it will be directing you up towards crime location 5, and approximately in this area here, that is where that general is referring to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. We've seen those on the video. Now, let's go to crime location 1. Not for you to tell us anything that other people said, but if this is the case where a single body without its head was found, just tell us this: Within the 60 or 62 statements that you've reviewed, was there any witness able to give any -- who might have been able to give any firsthand account of that killing? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that witness included in the five to which the 30 you had originally chosen has now been reduced?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to crime location 2, which you have split up into -- and we can see it, 2, 2.3, 2.4, and 2.5. How many deaths are associated with these four subdivided parts of crime location 2?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Crime location 2, scene 2, there are three bodies. Crime location 2, scene 3, there is one body. Crime location 2, scene 4, we have one body. And at crime location 2, scene 5, one body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's six bodies altogether. Just -- just yes or no to this. Within the statements you reviewed, were there live eyewitnesses to any part of this incident?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or more than one such witness?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has it been possible to include any of those in the five witnesses to come before court?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we now go up on the map to crime location 3, which you have divided up, or has been divided up, into three sublocations --

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, 3.6 and 3.7. Well, the legend speaks of 3.8, but is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, there are three locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the three locations. There's 6, there's 7, and there's 8. Does this crime location or is this crime location spoken of by one or more than one of the five witnesses coming to court?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or more than one?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that witness able to deal just with one of these sublocations or with more than one?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Agim Mehmeti.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, namely which locations can the --

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. Namely crime location 3, scene 7, and one part of crime location 3, scene 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on from location 3 to location 4. I should have asked you: How many deaths associated in those three crime locations, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Crime location 4, which you identify as a single scene, scene 9, any deaths associated there?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour; three deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any live witness coming to court capable of dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: There is, Judge. There's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Your Honour."

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one. And so that area is covered.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's got through two of the five witnesses?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to crime location 5, divided into scenes 10, 11, and 12 but certainly we can see -- well, we can see 10. Is this the central part of what happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. It is one -- it is one part -- one of the very serious parts of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the ravine?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many witnesses of the five coming to court are able to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many deaths associated with that area?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Twenty-three in crime location 5, scene 10, and one in each of 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So two witnesses for 5.10. Any witnesses amongst our five for 5.11 and 5.12?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we've got through four of our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fifth witness relates to what area? It may be you've forgotten one along the way, actually. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Let's just go across the map to number 6. And this is scene 13. How many deaths associated here?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any of our five witnesses able to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there included within the 60 witness statements you reviewed a live witness who would be able to deal with that in part in any event?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just go back to see which one you've missed. Take your time. You've told us two at 5, one at 3, and I think one at 4. Which is the missing one?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It's for this area here. We have a witness who is prepared to give an overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And can also deal with some of the events in the previous years?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now -- and I hope the Chamber will allow this question, although -- from this witness. We'll have a look at the format your report in a minute, not its content, but with five witnesses that you've selected or we've selected, is there, in your judgement, enough material to give a sequence of events overall happening in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there, from those five witnesses, enough material to cover comprehensively the activity of the KLA over the period of time?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there, from the witnesses selected, material to give an account of the involvement of such Serbian forces as may have been involved?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we consider very briefly the format of your report described an assessment -- do you have a copy of it there with you?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber could be good enough to turn, as an example, to page 4 of 66 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where you've been setting out the history as you were able to conclude it may have been of events, you footnoted in each case the witnesses who support the propositions that you're summarising.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that sometimes you can have one, two, three, four, five, six, seven witnesses supporting a proposition, as in footnote 5, sometime it can be a mere single witness, or potential witness, as in footnote number 8?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that pattern has been followed throughout in your report although there are certain passages of narrative where you are summarising events and you don't use footnotes, but by and large you use footnotes and take everyone to the source of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see that you've also been able to refer to other materials, telegrams and other documents, matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could now have before him the -- or a copy of As Seen As Told, Volume I. And while that's coming to you, we know that the OSCE prepared an extensive report which is now our Exhibit 106, and I'd like simply the introduction, which is Roman numerals XV, to be laid on the overhead projector, please, for people to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can take Roman numerals XV headed "Introduction" laid on the projector. If you can't find it, I'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: What page are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: XV. Right at the beginning, the tenth page in.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's being laid on the overhead projector and being focused on, tell us this: At the time that you prepared your report, had you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document speaks of various OSCE documents that were made available to the ICTY. Had you seen those documents at the time you made your report?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I had seen some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of them. Had they been, any of them, reviewed by any colleague of yours?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes. They were reviewed by our analyst for the team -- one of the analysts for the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look at the methodology of this document and see how it compares with the methodology you employed. If we pass our eyes down the left-hand column of Roman page numbered XV, we can see that at the foot of the paragraph headed "Methodology" is this quotation: "After the 20th of March, the human rights division was engaged in taking victim and witness statements from refugees. All of this data has been scrutinised by the OSCE." Your report in large part was also based on witness statements but different witness statements?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you been able to consider some of the OSCE witness statements and compare them with those taken by ICTY investigators?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is any -- are there any particular characteristics of one or the other? Is one longer and more detailed or shorter and less detailed than the other? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I would describe it that the ICTY statements would be longer and in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next paragraph speaks of extensive references by citation throughout this report to OSCE documents and refugee interview forms. I'm not sure that you've made in your report -- have you any references to OSCE documents?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It speaks of the material that has then been made available to the ICTY on a confidential basis. And on the right-hand side, if we look at the right-hand side, thank you very much, in the first new paragraph, this sentence: "Where information --" second sentence: "Where information is acknowledged by the interviewee to be hearsay rather than the statement of a direct victim or witness, this is noted, as are inconsistencies when interviewees differ." Can you just help us with how that practice compares with or differs from the practice you've employed? Hearsay and inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Well, if hearsay -- hearsay and inconsistencies were -- were in the statements, they would be recognised as such and noted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further down the same column, we come to: "Human rights officers have visited locations previously identified and conducted further interviews." Is that parallel to what you've done?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In reference to the use of analysts, have analysts worked on the material provided?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further down this column, please. Or move the book up a little bit. Forensic evidence and continuing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forensic investigation is referred to. Now, that's, I think, all I need turn to. There are two more pages of methodology, and the Court may want to know that the introduction refers to what is page 10 of the report where further methodological descriptions are to be found, and I think all of them really match what this witness was doing in his report. Mr. Kelly, at this stage, one further question which isn't covered in a statement or indeed in your report, but it's necessary that I tell the Court and indeed the accused about it, and I'll do it through you although it's only just come to our knowledge. The KL -- the live witnesses from Racak have started to arrive, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are they sophisticated urban people or are they country folk?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: They're country folk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you detect yesterday something in them which may have been observed in earlier witnesses right at the beginning of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Their reluctance to speak about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this something you were advised to consider and investigate so far as you could?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To track down, if there was a reason for that reluctance, what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, I did make inquiries from them, and I did source the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And having sourced the reason, did you also check on the -- the emotions, the considerations of the witnesses themselves?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you then put them in touch with someone?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: The village leader in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were they able to speak to the village leader this morning?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so far as you're now able to tell, is there any impediment in their way of giving evidence about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: No. The village leader advised them to speak the truth and to speak about everything in their statement and to answer any question put to them, and he reassured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, of course, the statements that you took at the time, or whenever you took them, and the statements that were taken by others before your arrival on the scene, because you only took some of the statements, they deal with the KLA, don't they?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your report has summarised what you can glean about the history and involvement of the KLA from all those statements independently taken?

utterances.speaker: BARNEY KELLY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's, I think, all I propose to ask of the witness at this stage. We haven't reviewed any of the photographs. They're in the binder. They are mostly, I think, self-explanatory, although of course, it's sometimes easier to have them reviewed in detail by a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How -- how do you put this evidence in front of us now, knowing what we've said about hearsay in the past, also about the Rule that a witness really cannot comment on the issues which we have to determine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if you want this debate to be in the presence of the witness or if you'd prefer him to withdraw. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it makes much difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I put the argument in the same way as I put on previous occasions, and it comes to this: In our respectful submission, evidence of the kind contained in this report has three values: First, it has value in itself, and we can see it from the format of this report. If 25 witnesses say the KLA were present, or 25 witnesses say the VJ were present, that must have some weight in itself. There's no rule against hearsay, it's a question of weight. Second, as I have already identified on earlier occasions in this Tribunal and in this case, the material provides a very valuable potential for the Chamber to check any provisional findings it may have made against an assessed body of material. I think the Chamber will probably recall the way I dealt with this earlier, and it's probably worth repeating. If provisional views were formed as to a sequence of events or to participation of a particular group and the Chamber were to find nothing inconsistent in the report of a witness such as this, or indeed in material such as the OSCE document, then there would be nothing to stand in the way and to cause it concern before confirming any provisionally made view it had. But if it were to find material in a report or in a similar document contrary to its initial preliminary view, then that would be pause for thought. And that might lead to the third and very great value of a report like this which points out precisely where additional material in the form of live evidence that could be called is available. Now, those are the three general propositions that I have always advanced as essential. I beg your pardon, as lying behind, frankly, the essential use of this sort of material in trials like this. But Racak is a paradigm case, stronger perhaps than others, although any conclusion favourable to the adduction of this type of evidence in this case should, in our respectful submission, apply elsewhere, but it is a paradigm case, because it is impossible, with the best will in the world for a case with this number of locations, with the number of issues that are going to arise quite obviously from the cross-examination already advanced, to be dealt with on five live witnesses. But even before the Chamber imposed the time limitations that it did, even before that, the team, even before my arrival, a fortiori, after it, the team recognised that there was more material necessary to prove the case fully than could possibly be accommodated by conventional -- by the time that would be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I ask you this, another approach: Does any of the proposed summarised witnesses give evidence as to crimes in relation to which the five live witnesses will not testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that's why I got the witness to tell us in relation to those crime scenes that were not covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not talking about crime scenes. I'm talking about allegations of crime in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're all crimes of a kind within in the indictment. They're all part of the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What crimes would not be covered by the -- what crimes as charged --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Other killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- would not be covered by the five live witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Crimes of other killings that those five witnesses cannot speak of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about -- I'm talking about a crime in concept. If you have the crime of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- persecution, of murder, what I'm asking is whether any of the proposed summarising witnesses or summarised witnesses gave evidence as to a kind of crime. I think that's a better way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A kind of crime in respect of which the five live witnesses will not testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a question I've specifically addressed. I suspect the answer to it is no. I suspect the generality is going to be covered. But our concern includes that there should be an adequate sampling of evidence both for the case as a whole and for locations on an individual basis, and thus it is that by having the five witnesses, only a small part of the scene will be covered. And back to why it's a paradigm case, it's not just the fact that these crimes are going to be covered, it's the order in which they happened and the inferences that the accused and others may wish to draw from that about who did what and to whom and whether the bodies were moved, and all sorts of things like that. And it's our respectful submission that it simply isn't really possible to do the exercise in relation to a crime location like this on the limited live material that the time restraints will allow us. I didn't ask Mr. Kelly, but I know what his answer would have been. Perhaps you'll take it from me. In order to give a comprehensive account of this, that is a broadly comprehensive account, would it be necessary to call the 60 witnesses? No. You could probably get away with about 30. We know that 30 witnesses simply isn't even worth raising as a possibility for being called in relation to one scene. It wouldn't do. But that doesn't free us from the duty of attempting to lay before this Chamber the best material; and in our respectful submission, it doesn't free the Chamber of a duty to consider the best material. And the best material in this sort of problem case is some live and all other available methodologically established material. Which is, of course, another reason why I got the witness to show the similarities between his methodology and the methodology of the already exhibited As Seen As Told. And it would of course be interesting and valuable, by any process of reasoning, to see whether a conclusion reached on one database, which is what this witness would do, would be broadly similar to or broadly dissimilar from that produced on a substantially different database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The distinction which is -- which has been made in the past about reports such as the OSCE one is that they were not produced for the purposes of litigation, whereas it may be said that this report is. Now, that may not be a matter which is conclusive, but it is a point. Mr. Nice, it occurs to me that it's -- we're past the time for a break. This clearly is a matter which is going to require some consideration and some argument, too. Now, what is the better way to proceed? I mean, we can do as much as we can with this today, but it does occur to me that we have the general coming in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there sense in the course, and it would give us the opportunity to reflect on the position, which we're going to need, and I doubt we'll come to a decision today, is there any sense in trying to interpose another witness now and coming back to this witness later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may well be, and I know that of the pending witnesses, one certainly is in a state of very considerable anxiety. Nothing to do, I think, with anything except it's the sort of person he is. And I don't know if he's the next one on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One has been bis'd. The one I was hoping to call, bis'd. One has been subject to the 92 bis'ing procedure. The man I was particularly concerned about is not, so, yes, we could call a witness immediately afterwards. The general, I haven't yet heard from Mr. Ryneveld, who is seeing him or speaking to him almost immediately, but the general had made it clear that he was leaving on a 9.00 flight on Thursday morning -- 7.00 flight on Thursday morning back to Canada where he had commitments. Between 10.30 and 1.45, you get just under three hours altogether, and if only part of it has been given live, one would hope that the time would be sufficient for cross-examination by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what we'll do is this: If Mr. Kelly would be good enough to stand down, we will -- we will interpose another witness, deal with the general tomorrow, and return to this issue on Thursday when we'll hear argument, of course, from both sides on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, then can I, without trespassing on your time but for the convenience and saving of time, distribute two sheets which contain typed-up versions but -- I have the source but it's not a very good copy -- typed up versions of part of the Argentine Juntas trial and some comments from Dutch criminal proceedings and Spanish law, to assist. And can I also to turn the attention -- I'll put it on the record for ease -- to two passages from Rutaganda and Bagilishema. In Rutaganda, first instance judgement, the paragraph numbers are 363, 369, 372, 380, 381, 436, 439; and Bagilishema, paragraph 781.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you hand them in and we'll take them. I think it's important we take the adjournment now. Mr. Kelly, would you remember, please, you are on oath, so don't speak to anybody about your evidence, if you would, during the adjournment. Would you be back when you're called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. With apologies to all, quarter of an hour. Can we be back, please, at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness be sworn and then we'll hear the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few things to say. First of all, when I went out during the break, I was told that the next witness is Avdiu Bilall. When I got back from the break a minute ago, they told me that the next witness is the witness who has just come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, today, there is chaos here, and everybody can see that. William Fulton came -- went away before he came in, and I couldn't even cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were stopped cross-examining him because you were wasting the time of the Court. You were refusing to accept the instruction of the Court. You were continuing in your argument. Now, we're going to hear this witness now, and you can cross-examine. Yes. No. We're not hearing any more objection. Time is too short for that at the moment. You can make your objection when you come to cross-examine. Yes. Let's hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Drita Emini.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And, Witness, do I understand correctly that you are 24 years old, you are a Muslim of Kosovo Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you were born and have lived all your life in Racak with your father, mother, and brothers and sisters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you work at home?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do I understand correctly that you have given two statements to the investigators of the ICTY, and a few days ago, you were -- you made an appearance before a presiding officer of the Tribunal, at which time you indicated that those statements were true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You have had a chance to review those statements? They were read to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, during the course of those statements, I believe at one point you also identified some colours of uniforms that were shown to you. Is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRITA EMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to read a brief summary. At the conclusion of that summary of what is contained in her statements, I would ask that the witness be shown one exhibit with respect to some colours of uniforms that she saw. If I may, then, Your Honours, to provide the Court and the larger audience a brief summary of what is contained in those statements. Drita Emini tells how in the two years prior to the 15th of January, Serb police would enter Racak and take people into the police station and beat them. On one particular occasion, two policemen took her father to the police station in Stimlje where he was beaten. In late 1998, she describes the positioning of Serb forces on the hills surrounding Racak and how, over a three to four-month period, Racak was fired upon on a daily basis from those hills. She describes how Serb forces arrested her neighbour and how, on the same day, Serb paramilitaries fired at herself and the members of her family as they ran to their neighbour's basement for shelter. She tells in her statement of a time when the witness and her family left Racak for three days for safety reasons, and on another occasion, they lived in a cave for six days to avoid the firing that was happening in Racak. In particular, however, she describes the events on the 15th of January, 1999. That morning, she indicates in her statement, that she was awakened at about 6.30 a.m. by the sound of shooting in the village. Through her bedroom window, she saw the police and the army located on some of the hills and up on the ravine. Moments later, her window was shattered by a bullet. The witness and her family fled and joined a group of some other 34 people in her uncle's basement where they sought shelter. She provides various lists. One of the lists she provides is a list of those people who were seeking shelter. In her statement as well, she describes at about 8.00 on that day, 8.00 a.m. on the 15th of January, 1999, Rame Bega, and Xhami Bega came to the basement and told how three members of their family had been killed trying to escape the police. She indicates that her cousin Ismet Emini arrived wounded at the basement, carrying what he said was a part of the bone of his brother's forehead. He apparently had died in his brother's arms from a bullet wound to the head. While in the basement, the witness could see the police firing into Racak. She saw that through a gap in the basement wall. She describes how at 12.00 a.m. - I take it that's noon - a policeman ordered them out of the basement. She describes groups of soldiers being present. She recalls seeing neighbours who had not been in the basement standing with their hands raised, and one of her neighbours, Bajram Mehmeti, lying on the ground. She fainted. The Serb forces accused younger men of being UCK, or KLA, members and describes some of the insults that were perpetrated at that time. She describes the separation of the women and children from the men and that she, along with the other women and children, were taken to a house under guard where, under threat of being killed, they remained all afternoon, listening to the shooting. Later, they saw an OSCE vehicle drive past, and her father told her that the men had been ordered to walk towards Bebushit hill, but they hid. The following morning, the 16th of January, her statement describes how she went on with other villagers to the ravine at Bebushit hill where she saw many bodies. She then provides a list of 38 names of those bodies she recognised, and she goes on to describe that she stayed with her cousin for three days, returned on the 19th of January and assisted the OSCE and located her missing brother. Those are basically a very, very general and brief description of what the witness saw. Might the witness be shown, Madam Clerk, the uniform recognition guide. I think it was Exhibit 17, or was it 18?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you have described seeing various police, and you were shown some photographs, and you made a selection of what some of the uniforms looked like that you saw.
